In [[geometry]], the '''Clifton–Pohl torus''' is an example of a [[compact space|compact]] [[Lorentzian manifold]] that is not [[geodesically complete]]. While every compact [[Riemannian manifold]] is also geodesically complete (by the [[Hopf–Rinow theorem]]), this space shows that the same implication does not generalize to [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]]s.<ref name="one">{{citation |title=Semi-Riemannian Geometry With Applications to Relativity |volume=103 |series=Pure and Applied Mathematics |first=Barrett |last=O'Neill |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |year=1983 |isbn=9780080570570 |page=193 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CGk1eRSjFIIC&pg=PA193 }}.</ref> It is named after Yeaton H. Clifton and [[William Francis Pohl|William F. Pohl]], who described it in 1962 but did not publish their result.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Wolf | first = Joseph A.
 | edition = 6th
 | isbn = 978-0-8218-5282-8
 | mr = 2742530
 | page = 95
 | publisher = AMS Chelsea Publishing, Providence, RI
 | title = Spaces of constant curvature
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=mITRODOqZNsC&pg=PA95
 | year = 2011}}.</ref>

== Definition ==
Consider the manifold <math>\mathrm{M} = \mathbb{R}^2 \smallsetminus \{0\}</math> with the metric
: <math>g= \frac{2\,dx\,dy}{x^2+y^2}=\frac{dx\otimes dy + dy\otimes dx}{x^2+y^2}</math>

Any [[homothetic transformation|homothety]] is an [[isometry (Riemannian geometry)|isometry]] of {{tmath| M }}, in particular including the map:
: <math>\lambda(x,y)=(2x, 2y)</math>

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be the subgroup of the [[isometry group]] generated by {{tmath| \lambda }}. Then <math>\Gamma</math> has a proper, discontinuous [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] on {{tmath| M }}. Hence the quotient {{tmath|1= T = M/\Gamma }}, which is topologically the [[torus]], is a Lorentz surface that is called the Clifton–Pohl torus.<ref name="one"/> Sometimes, by extension, a surface is called a Clifton–Pohl torus if it is a finite covering of the quotient of <math>M</math> by any homothety of ratio different from&nbsp;{{tmath| \pm 1 }}.

== Geodesic incompleteness ==
It can be verified that the curve
: <math>\sigma(t) := \left(\frac 1 {1-t},0\right)</math>
is a [[null geodesic]] of ''M'' that is not complete (since it is not defined at {{tmath|1= t=1 }}).<ref name="one"/> Consequently, <math>M</math> (hence also {{tmath| T }}) is geodesically incomplete, despite the fact that <math>T</math> is compact. Similarly, the curve
: <math>\sigma(t) := (\tan(t), 1)</math>
is also a null geodesic that is incomplete. In fact, every null geodesic on <math>M</math> or <math>T</math> is incomplete.

The geodesic incompleteness of the Clifton–Pohl torus is better seen as a direct consequence of the fact that <math>(M,g)</math> is extendable, i.e. that it can be seen as a  subset of a bigger Lorentzian surface. It is a direct  consequence of a simple change of coordinates. With
: <math>N =\left(-\pi/2,\pi/2\right)^2 \smallsetminus \{0\};</math>
consider
: <math>F : N \to M</math>
: <math>F(u,v) := (\tan(u),\tan(v)).</math>

The metric <math>F^*g</math> (i.e. the metric <math> g </math> expressed in the coordinates {{tmath| (u,v) }}) reads
: <math> 
 \widehat{g\,} =\frac{du\,dv}{\tfrac{1}{2}(\cos(u)^2\sin(v)^2+\sin(u)^2\cos(v)^2)}.
</math>

But this metric extends naturally from <math>N</math> to {{tmath| \mathbb R^2 \smallsetminus \Lambda }}, where
: <math> \Lambda =\left\{\tfrac \pi 2 (k,\ell)\ \mid\ (k,\ell)\in \mathbb Z^2, k+\ell\equiv 0 \pmod 2 \right\}. </math>

The surface {{tmath| (\mathbb R^2 \smallsetminus \Lambda, \widehat{g\,}) }}, known as the extended Clifton–Pohl plane, is geodesically complete.<ref name="BMCP">
{{citation 
 |last1=Bavard |first1=Ch.
 |last2=Mounoud |first2=P.
 |title=Surfaces lorentziennes sans points conjugués
 |journal=Geometry and Topology
 |volume=17
 |year=2013
 |pages= 469–492
 |doi=10.2140/gt.2013.17.469 |doi-access=free
}}
</ref>

== Conjugate points ==
The Clifton–Pohl tori are also remarkable by the fact that they were the first known non-flat Lorentzian tori with no [[conjugate points]].<ref name="BMCP"/> The extended Clifton–Pohl plane contains a lot of pairs of conjugate points, some of them being in the boundary of <math> (-\pi/2,\pi/2)^2</math> i.e. "at infinity" in {{tmath| M }}.
Recall also that, by [[Hopf–Rinow theorem]] no such tori exists in the Riemannian setting.<ref name="EHopf">
{{citation 
 |last=Hopf |first=E.

}}
</ref>
